keyVerseText: And Jeuz, and Shachia, and Mirma. These were his sons, heads of the fathers.
rootMeaning: The root of מִרְמָה (Mirmâh) is מִרְמָה (mirmâh), which conveys notions of craftiness, deceit, guile, and treachery. This root sense emphasizes subtlety and falsehood, suggesting a deliberate act of fraud or deception. Unlike the general English term "fraud," the Hebrew root carries a nuanced implication of cunning and intentional betrayal, highlighting the moral and ethical dimensions behind the act.
usageInScripture: The word מִרְמָה (Mirmâh) appears only once in Scripture as a proper name, specifically referring to a Benjamite born in the land of Moab. In this context, it is translated simply as "and Mirma," indicating a personal name rather than an abstract concept of deceit. This singular usage as a proper noun shows that while the root meaning involves fraud or deceit, the word itself can function as an identifier without carrying that negative connotation in every instance.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding מִרְמָה in its root sense of deceit and treachery is vital for grasping the biblical emphasis on truthfulness and integrity before God. The contrast between the root meaning and its use as a personal name reminds believers that names and words can carry deep moral weight, yet God’s sovereign purposes can work through individuals regardless of their names’ original meanings. This invites reflection on God’s grace to redeem and transform, even where human frailty and sinfulness are implied by language. It also underscores the seriousness with which Scripture treats deceit, calling the faithful to live transparently and honestly in their walk with God.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Chronicles 8:10, the name Mirma appears among the sons and heads of fathers, highlighting his role within the genealogical record of Benjamin. Here, the word functions simply as a proper name, detached from its root meaning of deceit. This illustrates how God’s providence encompasses all individuals, regardless of the linguistic implications of their names, and invites believers to look beyond surface meanings to God’s sovereign plan in history.
